tagline: Nine miles of 1940 freeway, still keeping its 1940 manners.
intro: Out of downtown Los Angeles the northbound lanes go through the Figueroa Street Tunnels under Elysian Park, cross the Los Angeles River and take up the Arroyo Seco, an intermittent stream out of the San Gabriel Mountains. The parkway keeps mostly to its west bank through Highland Park, then crosses over into South Pasadena and ends at Glenarm Street in Pasadena.

Most of it opened in 1940, the last Los Angeles stretch the day before the Tournament of Roses Parade. It was designed for 45 miles an hour, and many of its ramps are still tight right-hand turns to and from side streets.

moments.title: Figueroa Street Tunnels
moments.text: Northbound traffic still runs through four tunnels from the 1930s, built with Art Deco patterns and a stylized seal of Los Angeles over each of the eight openings.

moments.title: Santa Fe Arroyo Seco Railroad Bridge
moments.text: In Highland Park the parkway passes under a railroad bridge four decades older than itself, more than 710 feet long and 56 feet up, where Metro's A Line trains cross now.

moments.title: Pasadena
moments.text: The freeway quits at Glenarm Street, and the Arroyo Parkway carries on as a city street to Colorado Boulevard, the old Route 66.

practical: Trucks have been barred from the parkway since 1943.
